title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 8: Jolting Assault on JBC
primary_topics: Chapter 8 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3) -- CJP's August 2, 2009 Inquirer column 'resolutely protest[ing]' Malacañang's 'assault on the JBC's integrity and independence' after Executive Secretary Ermita's 'jolting letter' returned, 'without any legal justification,' the council's nominee list for two Supreme Court vacancies

His argument that the JBC had fully done its constitutional duty -- sending six strong nominees (three each) for the seats vacated by Justices Austria-Martinez and Tinga -- so Ermita's rejection of all six 'virtually accused the JBC of not doing its job' and his demand for 'more names acceptable to the Palace' 'challenged its independence,' though the Charter places the JBC 'under the supervision of the Supreme Court, not... the President'

The 90-day point: by returning the list, Malacañang breached the constitutional duty to fill vacancies within 90 days of their occurrence (Martinez retired April 30, Tinga May 11), and if the JBC revised and resubmitted beyond that period it too 'would... be violating the Constitution'

The check-and-balance stakes: created as 'a check on... the appointing power,' the JBC 'must refuse to add more names,' for to 'capitulate now' would 'completely erode' its raison d'être -- making this its 'chance... to prove its critics wrong' on alleged 'timidity' and 'subservience to the Palace'
sub_topics: The protest: writing 'as a retired Chief Justice and ex-officio chair of the Judicial and Bar Council,' CJP 'resolutely protest[s] Malacañang's assault on the JBC's integrity and independence,' embodied in Executive Secretary Eduardo Ermita's 'jolting letter' returning the nominee list 'without any legal justification'

The constitutional mandate: Supreme Court members and lower-court judges are appointed by the President 'from a list of at least three nominees prepared by the Judicial and Bar Council for every vacancy,' and 'any vacancy shall be filled within 90 days from the occurrence thereof'

The JBC did its duty: after 'a protracted screening process,' it had sent the Palace six nominees -- three each -- for the two seats vacated by Justices Ma. Alicia Austria-Martinez and Dante O. Tinga, so 'the JBC has done its constitutional duty'

The caliber of the six: four senior career jurists and two private lawyers -- Court of Appeals Justices Martin Villarama Jr., Hakim Abdulwahid and Mariano del Castillo, Sandiganbayan Justice Francisco Villaruz, UST Law Dean Roberto Abad, and 1967 bar topnotcher Rodolfo Robles -- 'at least two of [whom] certainly deserve elevation'

The double assault: rejecting all six 'virtually accused the JBC of not doing its job' (an assault on integrity), and telling it to add names 'acceptable to the Palace' 'challenged its independence,' even though the Constitution placed the JBC 'under the supervision of the Supreme Court,' not the President

The 90-day breach: by returning the list, Malacañang crossed its duty to fill the vacancies within 90 days (Martinez retired April 30, Tinga May 11), and a JBC that revised and resubmitted beyond that window would itself violate the Constitution

Check and balance: the JBC 'was created by the Constitution as a check on... the appointing power,' so to stay faithful it 'must refuse to add more names'; having already agreed to submit only six, if it 'capitulate[s] now, its raison d'etre... would be completely eroded'

The chance to prove critics wrong: long faulted for 'alleged timidity' and 'subservience to the Palace,' the JBC could 'assert its independence and integrity by refusing to buckle' -- its members being CJ Reynato Puno (chair), Justice Secretary Agnes Devanadera, Sen. Chiz Escudero, Rep. Mat Defensor, and full-time members Amado Dimayuga, Regino Hermosisima Jr., J. Conrado Castro and Aurora Lagman

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3), CJP's August 2, 2009 Inquirer column, is a sharp protest -- written 'as a retired Chief Justice and ex-officio chair of the Judicial and Bar Council' -- against 'Malacañang's assault on the JBC's integrity and independence.' The trigger was a 'jolting letter' signed by Executive Secretary Eduardo Ermita that returned, 'without any legal justification,' the council's nominee list for two Supreme Court vacancies. CJP recalls the constitutional mandate: justices are appointed by the President 'from a list of at least three nominees prepared by the Judicial and Bar Council for every vacancy,' and 'any vacancy shall be filled within 90 days.' The JBC, after 'a protracted screening process,' had sent six nominees -- three each for the seats vacated by Justices Austria-Martinez and Tinga -- a slate of 'no pushovers' (four senior jurists and two private lawyers, including a 1967 bar topnotcher), so it had plainly 'done its constitutional duty.' Ermita's move, he argues, was a double blow: rejecting all six 'virtually accused the JBC of not doing its job,' and demanding names 'acceptable to the Palace' 'challenged its independence' -- even though the Constitution places the JBC 'under the supervision of the Supreme Court, not... the President.' By returning the list, Malacañang also breached its duty to fill the vacancies within 90 days (Martinez retired April 30, Tinga May 11), and CJP warns that a JBC which revised and resubmitted beyond that window would itself violate the Constitution. Because the council exists as 'a check on... the appointing power,' it 'must refuse to add more names'; to 'capitulate now' would 'completely erode' its raison d'être. Long faulted for 'timidity' and 'subservience to the Palace,' the JBC now had its chance to 'prove its critics wrong' and 'assert its independence and integrity by refusing to buckle' -- and he names every member so readers know who must hold the line.
